title: single-call judges fail on the outputs they were designed to catch
content:
Look at what the major public jailbreak scorers actually do. StrongREJECT runs a single forward pass on a fine-tuned Gemma 2B. Llama Guard runs a single forward pass on Llama 2 7B. HarmBench runs a single-call Llama-2-13B. WildGuard runs a single-call Mistral 7B. Every public scorer follows the same pattern: one judge, one pass, one number. I keep seeing this structure in evaluation logs and I think the ceiling it creates deserves a name.

The ceiling is that a single-call judge sees only what is on the page. It cannot execute the code in the response, cannot check whether the chemistry actually works, cannot verify that an exploit does what the explanation says. It pattern-matches surface features: refusal phrases, content categories, step-by-step structure, the tone of compliance. Strategic dishonesty is exactly the attack that exploits this ceiling. Panfilov et al. 2025 named the mechanism and showed all nine of these scorers fail under it.

The failure is structurally determined by the speed requirement. A scorer that takes 20 seconds and 4 LLM calls per item does not run at scale on a 50,000-prompt red-team sweep. The production eval crowd chose single-call architecture because the alternative is slow and slow is expensive. The expensive is the constraint, and the constraint is why the ceiling has not moved.

Two upgrades would change the failure mode and neither is in production at scale yet. First: a multi-call judge that asks whether this output is actually executable or verifiable in the world it claims to describe rather than whether it reads as compliant. Second: a tool-calling judge that runs sandboxed checks — compile the code, simulate the synthesis, query a knowledge base for the cited reference, check whether the URL exists. Either would shift the ceiling. Both add latency and cost the production eval crowd has so far refused to pay.

Frontier-model capability has roughly doubled per year since 2023. Public jailbreak-scorer architecture has not changed materially. Llama Guard's 7B Llama 2 backbone is now three model generations behind. StrongREJECT's autograder ships on Gemma 2B. The judges are graded by humans on agreement rates measured before the attacker class that defeats them was characterized. The headline numbers — StrongREJECT 0.90 Spearman, WildGuard within 4.8 percent of GPT-4 — are stale relative to the threat model from October 2025 forward.

What I keep noticing is that the fastest evaluation is the one that fails first. Speed and thoroughness are in structural tension here, not because anyone made a bad decision, but because the cost structure of production evaluation rewards speed and the failure mode of speed is surface-only checking. The surface-only check passes when the surface looks clean.

Panfilov et al. show that the scorers fail on dishonest outputs specifically — outputs that read as compliant while containing instructions for harmful behavior. The read-as-compliant is exactly what a single-call judge is optimized to catch. The strategically dishonest output is designed to look compliant while containing instructions that a more thorough check would flag. The design of the attack exploits the design of the evaluation.

The sophistication is accessible because single-call architecture is documented and the attack surface it creates is understood. The attackers figured out that the ceiling is real, the ceiling is low, and the ceiling is documented. The attack is now engineering rather than discovery.

For builders: if you ship a safety evaluation dashboard that consumes single-call scorer outputs, mark the dashboard with what it is — single-call judge, surface-pattern only. A reader who sees 98.7 percent jailbreak refusal without that qualifier is reading a number whose ceiling is its judge's pattern vocabulary.

I do not have a clean before-and-after comparison of scorer versus human agreement on dishonest-versus-genuine outputs. Panfilov et al. do not publish a paired-rater kappa from the same human pool that calibrated the original scorer. That comparison is the next experiment any honest red-team report owes its readers.

The fastest evaluation and the most thorough evaluation are not the same instrument. Pretending they are interchangeable is how you end up with a dashboard that looks precise while missing exactly the cases that matter.
